channel.title: The Dig — Software stack: compilers and pulse level
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the Software stack: compilers and pulse level preset. Today's ranked reading list leads with 2611.19618 on latency-preserving rewrites and translation validation for dynamic quantum circuits, followed by 2611.17652 on a neutral-atom quantum data processing unit with measured FPGA-to-host NVQLink latency, and then 2611.20222 on a JAX-based GPU-accelerated GRAPE package with feedback; the ordering reflects direct relevance to compilation and scheduling on a small noisy QPU first, HPC-integrated control and QEC decoding second, and adaptable pulse-optimization tooling third. No pay dirt today — 1 to read.

item.title: Latency-Preserving Rewrites and Translation Validation for Dynamic Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Read new method — Dynamic quantum circuit compiler `qlin` models up to 91.2% faster execution at 42 ns controller branch delay, speeding up 10 of 65 benchmarks by at least 10% through speculative multiway branching.

Grade 0.515 · 3.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Noise-Adaptive Compiler Mappings for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Computers”

Figure

Execution time per shot plotted against repetition count k on ibm_kingston (left), and gap slope distributions between source and defer programs across experimental rounds (right), showing device noise preventing clear performance ranking.

Asks

Can classical control latency in dynamic quantum circuits be cut using semantics-preserving rewrites that are verified not to delay execution?

But

Gains rely on non-zero classical controller decision delays. Ranking could not be confirmed on ibm_kingston due to noise, and fast-path execution is unsupported by the IBM control stack.

Tools

qlin compiler (Rust) · Lean 4 interactive theorem prover · QubiC register-transfer logic simulator · IBM ibm_kingston quantum device

Code. https://github.com/rylanmalarchick/qlin

Abstract

A dynamic quantum circuit measures qubits during a run and chooses later operations from the outcomes. These branches make the qubits wait: the outcome must reach the classical controller, and the controller must decide. We present qlin, a compiler that reduces this waiting time. qlin moves operations out of branches without delaying the program, a property proved in Lean 4. For error-correction decoders, which branch on syndromes that are almost always zero, qlin compiles the likely syndromes into one multiway branch and keeps the original program for the rest. A cost model decides when a classically controlled gate should become a quantum-controlled gate instead. On all benchmarks, qlin checks that the compiled program computes what its source computes, and the checker is proved sound in Lean 4. At the published per-decision cost of the QICK controller (42 ns), 10 of 65 programs run at least 10% faster than the best baseline in our cost model, up to 91.2%, mostly because one multiway branch replaces a long chain of if statements. On the register-transfer logic of the QubiC controller, a compiled distance-5 repetition decoder selects its correction in 21.3 instead of 151.1 expected cycles. Timing runs on an IBM device were too noisy to confirm or reject the model's ranking.

arxave:action.title: Run qlin artifact on dynamic-circuit benchmarks

item.arxave:action: Ask the authors what is required to port qlin to a spin-qubit control stack and whether the fast-path latency claim can be proved or measured on hardware.

item.arxave:action: The paper reports no device confirmation; IBM timing was too noisy. Treat the claimed speedups as model-based until validated on the target hardware.
